yes_case.case: The closest past historical episodes are the 2017 decision to standardize financial and intermediary services under the unified GST framework and the subsequent 2019-2021 clarifications regarding IT-enabled services and banking outsourcing fees. In those past episodes, the GST Council initially hesitated to tax business-to-business financial integration layers due to fears of cascading taxation on credit delivery. However, this current episode differs crucially in the Council's aggressive posture toward modern fintech-NBFC partnerships and co-lending arrangements; unlike the passive stance on legacy banking outsourcing, the state revenue deficits and the rapid explosive growth of un-taxed co-lending credit lines have created an urgent fiscal imperative. Furthermore, previous rate-tightening episodes targeted peripheral financial services, whereas this specific 18% levy directly targets the core arbitrage mechanism between regulated banks and shadow-banking NBFCs, making it a distinct tightening cycle driven by revenue maximization rather than mere administrative clarification.
key_evidence: The 2017 foundational GST standardization of financial services
The 2019-2021 rulings on banking outsourcing and intermediary fees
The structural shift toward targeting modern co-lending credit arbitrage channels
yes_case.strength_reason: The historical precedent shows a clear trajectory of the GST Council gradually closing loopholes on financial sector intermediaries, and the current focus on NBFC-to-bank services is the logical continuation of past tax-base expansions, differentiating itself only by the higher fiscal desperation of the current Council.
yes_case.deliberately_ignored: I have completely left aside all modeling of exact tax revenue yields, procedural voting dynamics within the GST Council meetings, the exact timeline of upcoming Council sessions, and any legal probability assessments of court challenges.

no_case.case: The closest past episodes are the 2019-2020 GST Council deliberations on priority sector lending certificates (PSLCs) and the 2022 clarification regarding GST applicability on certain guarantees provided by directors. In both of those historical episodes, the Council faced acute revenue-protection pressures from state governments and actively sought to expand the tax net to intermediate financial transactions. However, this episode differs fundamentally because the proposed levy targets the specific architecture of NBFC-bank co-lending arrangements, a systemic credit channel that regulators are currently trying to nurture rather than constrain. Unlike the PSLC taxation—where the market was mature and the tax incidence was easily absorbed—applying an 18% GST directly to NBFC-to-bank intermediation services threatens to structurally break the co-lending model by creating an insurmountable cascading tax cost that cannot be claimed as input tax credit efficiently by banks. Furthermore, unlike the director-guarantee case which targeted closely held corporate governance loopholes, taxing NBFC-bank services strikes at the core of systemic liquidity transmission to priority sectors, making the political and economic friction far higher than in the historical tax-expansion episodes.
key_evidence: The 2019-2020 GST Council treatment of Priority Sector Lending Certificates (PSLCs) where intermediate financial instruments were brought under the tax net.
The 2022 GST Council clarification on corporate and director guarantees creating taxable supplies of services.
The current operational reliance of banks on NBFCs for last-mile credit delivery via co-lending frameworks.
no_case.strength_reason: The structural and economic resistance to taxing a vital credit-transmission channel makes this episode distinct from past revenue-driven tax expansions on isolated financial instruments.
no_case.deliberately_ignored: Voting majorities of state finance ministers, precise revenue collection targets, statutory timelines of upcoming GST Council meetings, and macro-level statistical compliance rates.

I adjusted the probability downward from the outside view to 58% to reflect the high friction identified in the 'No' case, while maintaining a majority probability due to the persistent fiscal pressure on state governments to expand the GST net.
